POLICEMAN SHOOTS
FUGITIVE FOOTPAD
Negro, Hit by Two Bullets, Runs Until He Drops Unconscious.
PHILADELPHIA, Aug. 7.—With a policeman on guard at either side of his cot in the Pennsylvania Hospital, Charles Smith, a negro, who says his home is in Detroit, lies in a serious condition, with two bullets in his body.

Policeman Markey, while standing at the corner of Ninth and Clinton streets early today, heard a man shout "Murder!" He found a white man struggling in the grip of two regroes, who were going through his pockets. Both ran.

Markey ran after one, who gained. The policeman fired two shots. The negro dropped, arose, and ran. A third shot was fired, but the negro ran until he dropped insensible.

When the police returned to the scene of the hold-up they found the victim of the negroes had gone.

de-quincey-de-quincey-1910-07-31.A1:
More Trouble for Negroes
Beaumont, Tex., July 31.—One negro was killed outright and another painfully wounded, and a negro woman perhaps fatally wounded at DeQuincey, La., last night by an unknown assassin. The three negroes were seated in a tent on the Frisco railroad yesterday when three shots from a shotgun loaded with buckshot were fired into the tent from the darkness. There is no clue.
de-quincey-de-quincey-1910-07-31.A2:
RESISTS CAB FARE ORDINANCE. Taximeter Co. Says the Aldermen Are Trying to I surp Powers. The Universal Taximeter Cab Company, which has a stand in front of the Hotel Knickerbocker, asked for an injunction yesterday which would prevent the city from enforcing the new ordinance reducing the fares of taxicabs from 50 cents to 40 cents for the first half mile. The company says that it would lose $1,300 a month, that it is doing a private business and that the Board of Aldermen has no power to fix prices in a private business. The motion was put over until to-morrow, when it will be argued before Justice Bischoff. AMUSEMENTS. NEGROES KILLED IN CAMP. Unknown Persons Fire Fifty Shots Into a Tent Full of Laborers.
NEW ORLEANS. Aug. 1. Unknown parties fired from the woods into a camp of negroes working for the Frisco Railroad at De Quincey, in Calcasieu parish, Louisiana, last night, killing two and seriously wounding two. There were twenty negroes in the tent at the time, and the tent was riddled with bullets, more than fifty shots being fired.

There has been much feeling in the De Quincey neighborhood, which is a white section, because of the employment of negro labor by the Frisco Railroad, and there was a similar shooting affray some time ago.
de-quincey-de-quincey-1910-07-31.A3:
BLACK KILLED FOLLOWING TROUBLES.
Lake Charles, La., Aug. 1.—As a result of the trouble that has been brewing for some months on account of the negro labor employed by the Colorado Southern railroad, the negroes employed at the car shops at De Quincey, fifteen miles northwest of Lake Charles, were fired upon early yesterday morning, one of the blacks being killed instantly, a negro woman fatally wounded and several negro men badly hurt.
de-quincey-de-quincey-1910-07-31.A6:
HATTIESBURG, MISSISSIPPI, TUESDAY AFTERNOCN. AUGUST 2. I910.
FUSILLADE POURED
INTO NEGRO TENT
One Killed, One Mortally Wounded And Two Others Hurt.—Authorities Investigating.
Special to The News.
Lake Charles, La., Aug. 2.--More than fifty shots were fired from ambush Saturday night by unknown parties into a tent occupied by negroes near the Frisco shops at DeQuincey, twenty miles north of Lake Charles, and as a result Will McMillin, a negro employe of the road, was instantly killed; Susie Johnson was shot through the head and mortally wounded and two other negroes received bullets, one through the shoulder and another in the arm.

At the time of the shooting there were twenty negroes in the tent. Sunday was given over to an investigation of the shooting by officers from Lake Charles, but no arrests have been made so far.

Several theories are put forward showing a motive for the crime. By some it is believed that the attack followed a quarrel among the negroes themselves. Others say that considerable friction over the employment of negro labor in the Frisco shops at DeQuincey has been evident for several months. Several days ago a Frisco brakeman beat up a white man, and this, it is contended, may have fanned the flame of race feeling.

Alma Kellner, eight years old, was caught in San Francisco. He was found hiding under a sink in a rooming house in that city. He admitted his identity but denied slaying the Kellner child.

SPORTING AFFAIRS. Jack Sheridan, the veteran umpire, who recently retired from active service on the American league staff, visited President Johnson in Chicago to receive instructions for the new duties which will devolve upon his shoulders. Sheridan is to hold forth in a new role from now on. In a way the veteran will serve as chief of the umpires, and at the same time will travel around the country in quest of new and promising talent for umpires.

F. H. Whitley, holder of the motorcycle championship of the United States, will not be permitted to compete in the annual championship races in Philadelphia next month. He has been suspended from membership indefinitely by the officers of the Federation of American Motorcyclists. Whitley appeared in the Salt palace, a National Cycling association track in Salt Lake City. Representatives of the federation, which are at outs with the association, consulted the eastern headquarters by telegraph and Whitley's suspension followed.

James J. Jeffries has spiked the story that he was drugged at Reno. "I don't know who started this yarn about being drugged," said Jeffries at Los Angeles. rounds. In the seventh round the Japanese got his hold and Lennon was forced to quit.

Joe Hyland had a shade the best of Jack Dorman in a ten round boxing bout at Brown's gymnasium in New York. Dorman was not in good condition. He had only been in training a few days, preparing for his bout with Leach Cross, when he was offered the bout with Joe Hyland.

Rear Admiral James Albert Hawke, retired, of Bristol, Pa., formerly medical director of the navy, died at the Naval Medical School hospital in Washington. He was sixty-nine years old and during the civil war he served as surgeon to the Two Hundred and Fifteenth Pennsylvania volunteers.

James Ross Curran, vice president and one of the founders of the Carnegie Trust company, died at his home in New York. He was fifty-nine years old and during his career he held many important positions, at one time being president of the New York City Trust company.

TWO KILLED AT PINE CAMP
Negro Soldiers Fatally Shot in a Fight in a Hotel.
Pine Camp, N. Y., Aug. 29.—Private Turner, of Company B, 24th Regiment, and Corporal Jones, of Company C, were shot and instantly killed in a fight to-night in the ballroom of the Freeman House, at Great Bend, a hamlet near Pine Camp, where both soldiers were stationed. The dead men are negroes. Private McGee, of Troop L, 10th Cavalry, ran from the ballroom after the shooting, and officers are searching for him.
perry-mcgee-boonville-1910-08-30.A2:
NEGRO SOLDIER SLAYER IS CAPTURED WITH BULLETS.
Shoots at Police in Pursuit Rather Than Surrender.
UTICA, N. Y., Aug. 30.—Private Perry McGee, of Troop L, Tenth U. S. Cavalry, who shot and killed Private Turner, of Company B, Twenty-fourth Regiment, and Corporal Jones, of Company C, of the Twenty-fourth, at Great Bend, near Watertown, was captured at Boonville, twenty-five miles north of here, today. In a running fight with civil officers before he gave up he was probably fatally shot. McGee and his victims are negroes.

When the 8 o'clock train drew in Deputy Sheriff Wetmore and Constable Studor spied McGee on the bumpers. The soldier started up the tracks on a run, the officers following. Two residents of the village tried to stop him, but McGee drew his big cavalry pistol and for a while stood them off. Others joined in the chase and McGee was cornered between the canal and a knitting mill, after running several hundred yards.

Pressed Closely by the crowd he jumped into the water, and, standing waist deep, turned the gun on his pursuers. Studor told him to surrender. McGee shot at him. Studor returned the fire and then Walter Rinkle came up with a rifle. Both Rinkle and Studor fired at the same time, and the negro dropped with two bullets in his back. Physicians say he cannot live.
perry-mcgee-boonville-1910-08-30.A3:
NEGRO KILLS TWO;
CAUGHT IN WATER
Fires Upon Officer, Jumps Into Canal and Keeps Weapon Above Surface For Use.
SYRACUSE, N. Y. Aug. 30. Charged with the murder of Corporal Jones and Private Turner, of the Twenty-fourth Infantry, U. S. A. (negro), Trooper McGee, of the Tenth Cavalry, also a negro, was arrested to-day near Boonville by the sheriff and a detail of soldiers.

McGee was in the ballroom of the Freeman House at Great Bend late last night with a party of his comrades, when the infantrymen came in. There was a free-for-all fight, in which it is alleged that McGee shot both Jones and Turner. He claims he acted in self-defense.

The capture of McGee was dramatic. Constable Studor and Deputy Sheriff Wetmore saw him alight from a freight train and ordered him to halt. In reply, McGee opened fire. The officers sent four bullets into the negro's back. McGee jumped into the canal, holding his gun above the water. The officers covered him, drew him out of the water and rushed him to the Boonville jail, where it was said he would die.

The soldier started up the tracks on a run, the officers following. Two residents of the village tried to stop him, but McGee drew his big cavalry pistol and stood them off. Others joined in the chase and McGee was cornered between the canal and a knitting mill. Closely pressed he jumped into the water and standing waist deep turned the gun on his pursuers. Studor told him to surrender. McGee shot at him. Studor returned the fire and Walter Rinkle came up with a rifle. Both Rinkle and Studor fired at the same time and the Negro dropped with two bullet holes in his back. Physicians say he cannot live.

remus-white-1910-07.A1:
CHASE FOR NEGRO ENDS ALBERT JOHNSON CAUGHT IN LOWER ESCAMBIA. Wanted in Connection With Death of Jesse Baldwin Near Evergreen. Gives Statement Implicating Others.
Evergreen, Aug. 4.—(Special)—Albert Johnson, the negro wanted in connection with the murder near here several weeks ago of Jesse Baldwin, an aged farmer who lived alone in an isolated neighborhood, was captured today by Sheriff J. F. Irwin, near Gryas Creek in the lower part of Escambia county.

Sheriff Irwin's capture ended a chase of a month which carried him over nearly all of Florida and South Alabama, and which was made at an expense of several hundred dollars.

It is said that Johnson has made a statement to the effect that the fatal blow with the hoe was struck by Thomas White, a negro who was killed a few days after the tragedy by a shot fired by Deputy Sheriff Nalls. Johnson also implicated several others in the murder, it is claimed.

The negro was brought to the Conecuh county jail here this evening. The excitement which was caused at the time of Jesse Baldwin's murder has entirely subsided, and no violence is anticipated.
remus-white-1910-07.A2:
Negro Murderer Captured
Bay Minette, August 4.—(Special.)—Word has been received here that a negro answering the description of the one who murdered Jesse Baldwin of Conecuh county, near Wilcox, about a month ago, was captured this morning by Riley Hubbard, section foreman, between Bay Minette and Almore, on the Louisville and Nashville railroad, at about 8:30 o'clock. After the capture the negro confessed the crime and named three others who were implicated in the affair. Sheriff Irwin of Evergreen was notified at once and met Deputy Sheriff McGill, into whose hands the negro was placed, at Pollard.
remus-white-1910-07.A3:
SOLDIERS OF CONECUH GUARD BLACK QUINTET Mob Surrounds Jail at Evergreen. THREATEN VIOLENCE FOR DEATH OF JESSE BALDWIN When Troops Appear, Angered Citizens Disperse. SHERIFF IRWIN COMES TO MONTGOMERY SATURDAY MORNING, THINKING DANGER OF LYNCHING OVER AFTER FIRST ARREST.
Evergreen, Aug. 7.—(Special.)—At 3 o'clock this morning the streets of Evergreen in the vicinity of the Conecuh County jail are being patrolled by members of Company "K," 1st regiment, Alabama National Guard, of Evergreen, under command of Capt. T. M. Bruner.

Leaving the city in a northerly direction is a body of 100 or 125 men, who, during the early hours of the night, surrounded the Conecuh County jail, fired occasional shots, and hinted at violence against five negroes held in connection with the death of Jesse Baldwin, an aged farmer, who was murdered at Wilcox Station, July 7.

The mob formed at 12:30 o'clock, and did not disperse until after 3 o'clock, when the military assumed charge of the situation. It is believed that the members of the mob are from the country sections, and not from Evergreen.

When it was found that a mob was forming, the Evergreen troops were ordered into their armory. With them were Deputy Sheriffs E. C. Hinds and H. F. Nalls. These had the keys to the jail.

Jesse Baldwin's body was found near the back door of his home one month ago, his skull crushed by a blow from a hoe. He was known to have kept large sums of money about his home, and this money was missing. Conecuh County officers have been working on the case, and have captured five suspects. Albert Johnson was taken Wednesday in the lower part of Escambia County, and returned to Evergreen by Sheriff Irwin. Charley Henderson, another negro, was captured Friday. John Manuel, Charley Manuel and Jerry Mims, three other negroes, were taken and placed in jail Saturday morning.

The jail about which the mob assembled is considered almost mob proof. It is a two-story structure, about 40 by 60 feet in dimension. The outer door is of steel and opens outward. Behind that is another steel door which opens inward. To reach the cells, it is necessary to climb a winding stairway and open another steel door against which it is impossible to direct any kind of a battering ram.

Sheriff Irwin came to Montgomery Saturday night, and was at a local hotel when news of the mob was conveyed to him. He declared that he had expected trouble several nights during the last week, but believed that the excitement had subsided when he left Evergreen Saturday. He declared that there was no evidence of feeling when he left the town Saturday afternoon.

The Conecuh Sheriff expressed confidence in the two officers in charge, and also in the military force. He believed that the officials would be able to cope with the situation. He made preparations to leave Montgomery for Evergreen on the early morning train Sunday.
remus-white-1910-07.A4:
THE WEATHER. Washington, Aug. 7--Forecast for Alabama: Local showers Monday and Tuesday; light to moderate variable winds. RUSH NEGROES FROM CONECUH Prisoners Taken to Mobile Jail. TROOPS RELIEVED FROM DUTY Another Suspect Arrested by Members of Company. AUTHORITIES IN CONTROL OF SIT-UATION, AND BELIEVE DANGER OF LYNCHING DISAPPEARED WITH NEGROES' RE- MOVAL.
ing that another attempt would be made by a mob to storm the Conecuh county jail and lynch two negro men who were held there on a charge of having murdered Jesse Baldwin, an aged man on his farm near Wilcox about a month ago, Sheriff H. F. Irwin Sunday secured permission from Circuit Judge J. C. Richardson at Greenville, to remove Albert Johnson and John Manuel, the two negroes, to the Mobile county jail for safekeeping. The negroes were taken to Mobile Sunday afternoon by Sheriff Irwin and Deputy Sheriff Hinds.

When the 9:40 train from Montgomery arrived in Evergreen Sunday morning, Lieutenant J. C. Cheney, Jr., and Private G. R. Farnham, Jr., members of Company "K," went into a coach in which several negroes were riding and arrested Frank Mitchell, who is charged with having alced and abetted Albert Johnson and John Mitchell and John Manuel in evading arrest by the sheriff of Conecuh county. Mitchell was taken immediately to the Conecuh county jail, and there locked up with Charley Manuel, Jerry Mims and Charley Henderson, all negroes, who also are charged with having alded the two alleged murderers in evading arrest for several days.

Remus White, the third negro who was accused of taking part in the murder of Jesse Baldwin, was shot and killed several days ago by a deputy sheriff, who was in the act of arresting him.

Mob Came From North.

It was stated in Evergreen today that the mob of Saturday night came from the vicinity of Owassa and from the neighborhood in which Baldwin had lived prior to his murder. There, feeling is said to be bitter against the negroes. There were about 100 members in the mob, each one armed either with a shotgun or a Winchester rifle. Had not the local company of militia formed a protecting line about the jail before the arrival of the mob, serious consequence might have resulted.

Train No. 3 which arrived in Evergreen 10:45 o'clock Saturday night brought the information from Owassa that a large crowd of men, armed and on foot, would soon attack the county jail with a view to lynching all the negroes concerned in the murder of Jesse Baldwin.

This report reached Captain T. M. Bruner of Company "K," A. N. G., and he immediately called together all the available members of his company to arm themselves and report for duty at the jail.

While the members of the militia company, along with deputy sheriff were in the company armory, several members of the mob came into the room, and demanded that the deputy sheriff turn over to them the keys to the jail, according to Lieutenant Cheney and other members of the company. This was refused, and the members of the mob were ordered to get out of the building. No member of the militia recognized the men, although they were not masked.

The militia men then hurried to the jail, and had hardly formed a protecting line about the prison when the mob appeared. When the mob come within forty feet of the line of soldiers they were ordered to halt, and send one man forward to arbitrate with Captain Bruner. This was done. the mob leader whose name would not be divulged, asking that the keys to the jail be turned over to him. Again this demand was refused, and the refusal was accompanied by an order to the mob to disperse.

Trouble is Threatened.

At this juncture it seemed that trouble of a serious nature would occur, as the members of the mob began cocking their guns and mumbling in dissatisfied tones, according to statements of the militia men. After about half an hour, however, the mob quietly dispersed and disappeared in a northerly direction.

The militia was then disbanded, Lieutenant Cheney and Private Farnham being left on duty to guard the jail in case any members of the mob should return.

No further trouble was experienced however, and at 2:20 o'clock Sunday afternoon Lieutenant Cheney and Private Farnham formed a military escort and accompanied Deputy Sheriff Hinds with Albert Johnson and John Manuel as his prisoners to the railroad station. Sheriff Irwin coming from Montgomery, remained on the train and accompanied Deputy Hinds and the negroes to the Mobile county jail at Mobile.

Although some rumors were abroad in Evergreen during the early afternoon Sunday that a mob much larger than that of Saturday night, would storm the jail Sunday night, county officials were of the opinion that the removal of Johnson and Manuel against whom feeling was bitterest, to Mobile, would serve to deter such action.

Confesses Presence at Crime.

Mobile, Aug. 7.—Albert Johnson, the negro who, with John Manuel, is charged with the murder of Jesse Baldwin three weeks ago near Evergreen, and who was brought, with Manuel, to this city today by Sheriff Irvin of Conecuh County, after having escaped the wrath of a mob which ineffectually stormed the jail at Evergreen, confessed today that he was at the scene of the murder when Jesse Baldwin was done to death. He accused Manuel of having struck some of the blows which ended fatally for the aged farmer, and also stated that Remus White used a hoe on the old man, thus equally aiding in causing his death.

Shortly after the arrival here of Sheriff Irvin with his prisoners, a local reporter, in the presence of several deputy sheriffs, asked Johnson and Manuel whether or not they had had any hand in the killing of Jesse Bald-

accused of being one of the murderers, admitted that he was at the house of Baldwin when the old farmer was killed, and that he saw the murder committed, but he said he did not strike a blow, but merely looked on while the others did the killing. When he was asked who did strike the blow that killed the old man, he pointed at John Manuel and said that he was the one who had the club with which part of the killing was done; and that Remus White, the negro who was killed by Deputy Sheriff Noel three weeks ago, was the man who had the hoe, one of the weapons with which the crime was committed. As soon as Johnson finished telling this part of the story, Manuel called him a liar, and said that he (Manuel) had not been present at the killing at all. Sheriff Irvin stated that he would not be surprised if Johnson told the truth, as he believed that the killing had been done by more than one man.
remus-white-1910-07.A8:
BY THE SOLDIERS
Attack on Jail Checked in Alabama.

Evergreen, Ala., August 7. —Order was restored this morning here and Company K. First Infantry, of this place has been removed from duty. Fearing a further outbreak tonight, Sheriff J. F. Irwin and Deputy Sheriff E. C. Hinds this afternoon took Albert Johnson and John Manuel to Mobile for safe-keeping. These two negroes are held in connection with the murder of Jesse Baldwin, an aged farmer at Wilcox station July 7th.
Charley Henderson, Charley Manuel and Jerry Mims, three other negroes, remain in the jail in connection with the same case, but it is believed that the authorities are in full control of the situation, and that friends of the dead men will allow the law to take its course. The mob formed Sunday morning at 12:30 o'clock. Surrounding the jail the members fired shots and made threats against the black prisoners. The Evergreen company of infantry immediately was called to the armory. At 3 o'clock the mob was dispersed when the troops appeared and surrounded the jail, where they were on guard until the danger of the attack was passed.
remus-white-1910-07.A9:
NEGRO CONFESSED TO THE MURDER.
Mobile, Ala., August 7.—Albert Johnson, the negro who, with John Manuel, is charged with the murder of Jesse Baldwin, three weeks ago near Evergreen, Ala., and who was brought with Manuel to this city by Sheriff Irvin, of Conecuch county, after having escaped the wrath of a mob, confessed today that he was at the scene of the murder when Jesse Baldwin was done to death. He accused Manuel of having struck some of the blows which ended fatally for the aged farmer, and also stated that Remas White used a hoe on the old man, thus aiding in causing his death.

Johnson said that he did not strike a blow, but merely looked on while the other men did the killing.

As soon as Johnson finished Manuel called him a liar, and said that he (Manuel) had not been present at the killing at all.

NEGRO RIOTERS SCORED
HEAVY PUNISHMENT ASKED FOR POLICEMAN'S ASSAILANTS.
Attempt to Rescue Prisoners Who Profanely Objected to Being Moved On.
Last night's row near the Pennsylvania avenue bridge over Rock creek, when Policeman Johnston was attacked by a gang of fifteen drunken Foggy Bottom negroes, was described by Assistant United States Attorney Turner, in Police Court today, as one of the worst instances of lawlessness that has been brought to the attention of the United States attorney's office in a long time.

He asked the court to impose heavy penalties on the men arrested. Judge Aukam sentenced James Lomax to jail for sixty days, gave Richard Wallace forty-five days and Henry Nolden and Albert Brown thirty days each.

Johnson had ordered half a dozen negroes away from the moving picture theater at 28th and M streets. They became so profane that the policeman gave chase, arresting two offenders at the Georgetown end of the Pennsylvania avenue bridge.

When the policeman started for the patrol box the other members of the gang attempted a rescue. Johnson's night stick waswrenched from his hand and he was rather badly beaten up. He had to draw his revolver and fire in the air to frighten the negroes away.

Other members of the gang may be arrested today.

WASHINGTON, D. C., August 10.—Four negroes are in jail here to-day as the result of a race battle between one patrolman, three white citizens and fifteen negroes in the Georgetown district, where there has been almost constant race trouble since Johnson knocked out Jeffries. The negroes have threatened vengeance since two soldiers from Fort Myer shot down a negro three weeks ago. The news of the race war in Texas and the great "indignation meeting" held by negroes here Monday night has resulted in a situation so serious that the authorities to-day are confronted with a puzzling problem in their effort to find some way to prevent further trouble.

"This business is getting to the danger point," said a police official today. "Some one is going just a little too far, if it is not checked, and the national capital will be a scene of rioting that will not redound to the credit of the country."

Rush Police.

Patrolman I. H. Johnson, who is six feet three inches tall, ordered the negroes to "move on" when they blocked the sidewalk at Pennsylvania avenue and Twenty-sixth streets. They refused and rushed Johnson, who swung his night stick with telling effect. Three white men rushed to te policeman's aid and a general fight ensued, in which all sorts of weapons were used, from whiskey bottles to revolvers. As far as could be learned, however, no one was shot.

The negroes were finally put to flight, and three were captured. The captives yelled for help and the gang made a second rush, which probably would have resulted seriously if three policemen, attracted by the shooting, had not arrived on the scene. A third attack was made by the negroes, but with little effect, and they fled to "Foggy Bottoms," where the police allege a dangerous gang makes its headquarters.

WASHINGTON RACE RIOTS
Authorities in District of Columbia Fear Trouble Unless Turbulent Blacks Are Quelled.
Washington, Aug. 11.—Following another outbreak between negroes and whites in the Georgetown section the District authorities are fearful of real race riots in the capital.

Four negroes were arraigned in court charged with assaulting a policeman. In the fight that preceded their arrest shots were exchanged and stones and empty whisky bottles used with telling effect. The officials say unless radical action is taken to curb the lawless negroes at once, the situation may get beyond control.

Judge Chamberlain Clearing Docket of Mobile.

Mobile, Aug. 10.—(Special.)—There were forty-four cases of violating the prohibition law on the docket of the Inferior Criminal Court today. Some were nolle prossed at the instance of the solicitor; six were fined, three of whom appealed.

Judge Chamberlain has determined to get rid of this class of charges, and the docket tomorrow will show 100 additional ones. A number of those today were continued and the court hopes to clear the docket of them by the end of the week.

Bessie Cannon, the negress who interfered with Deputy Sheriff Bill Nugent Sunday in a box car at the time he killed William Beardsley, was today held for the action of the grand jury.

Nugent and Deputy Sheriff Stogsdill had a desperate struggle with the man who had the drop on them. The woman interfered with Nugent, while Stogsdill was having a hand to hand tussle with Beardsley for possession of the gun.

Beardsley was wanted for assaulting the Cannon woman's mother the latter part of last April.

Washington.—The ancient and long-established pass book system, used in ordinary savings institutions, will be adopted for the proposed postal savings banks when they are established by the United States government. The committee of officials that has been perfecting the plans for the postal banks had been considering what is known as the coupon system for postal bank deposits, but has now decided that, while having some advantages, that system might produce complications that would be undesirable.

Ackert May Succeed Rawn.

Lafayette, Ind.—At the office of the Monon here an unofficial report was made that Charles H. Ackert, now vice president of the Chicago & Alton railroad, would succeed the late Ira G. Rawn as president of the Monon. The story came from Washington, the headquarters of the Southern railroad. The stockholders of the Southern and the Louisville and Nashville roads hold the controlling interest in the Monon. Mr. Ackert was at one time superintendent of the Southern railroad at Knoxville, Tenn.

Cleveland.—Anthony Doyle, without money and too ill to ask for help, crawled into a doorway of a house, and while a busy crowd of men and women thronged by, struggled between life and death. A policeman shook the man but found him dead. The body was taken to the morgue. Two men, brothers of Doyle, called at the morgue and identified the dead man. The body was taken to an undertaker's room. Mrs. Anna Doyle, wife of the dead man, said that her husband was not old, in spite of his appearance—that he was but 39 years old.

New Philadelphia.—The local authorities are seeking persons who have threatened two prominent "drys" for their activities in the law enforcement campaign in Tuscarawas county. One letter threatens J. E. Hurst, editor of the Times.

Bellefontaine.—Friends here have received word of the deaths of John Shickendance and his son, Charles, who were shot by a policeman at Union City, Darke county, O. Policeman Jeff Conrad, who shot both men, was taken to jail at Greenville, charged with the double murder. He was later released on $8,000 bond. The officer tried to arrest the elder Shickendance on the charge of using profane language. The son and two sisters were returning from church when they heard the scuffle and running up, the son pulled the policeman off his father. Policeman Conrad fired four times, three bullets striking the elder Shickendance and one of them striking the young man, who was 21, while his father was 45 years old. Both of the victims of the officer's gun died later.

Ironton.—Congressman A. R. Johnson of the Tenth Ohio district, a Republican recently nominated, has just announced that he would withdraw because professional duties required all his time.

Cleveland.—The slipping of a pipe with which he was tightening a brake wheel sent August Anderson to his death over the brink of a precipice 60 feet high at the Bluestone quarries near South Euclid. Anderson is about 45 years old and lives in South Euclid. He was employed by the Murray Stone Co. at the Bluestone quarries. He was riding a flat car on the spur track that parallels the brink of the precipice and when nearing the destination of the car attempted to apply the brakes. To aid in putting on the brakes he made use of a heavy piece of pipe, inserting it between the spokes of the brake wheel. While exerting all his strength the pipe slipped from the wheel and Anderson, unable to save himself, plunged off the car and over the precipice.
